desc:
Write out all n suffixes of s (the suffix starting at index i is s[i..n)), sort them in ordinary dictionary order (a suffix that is a prefix of another one comes first), and return the start indices of the suffixes in that sorted order. This array is called the suffix array.

s = "banana"
suffixes sorted: a(5) ana(3) anana(1) banana(0) na(4) nana(2)
result = [5,3,1,0,4,2]

All suffixes have different lengths, so they are all different and the order is unique.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Sorting the suffixes as strings (sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: s[i:])) is correct, but the comparisons and the stored slices cost up to O(n2) characters, which hurts on strings like "aaaa..." and on larger inputs.

Sort by the first 1 character, then the first 2, then the first 4, then 8 ... Sorting by the first 2k characters needs only the order (rank) of the first k characters of the suffix at i and of the suffix at i + k.

Keep rank[i] for the current length k. Sort indices by the pair (rank[i], rank[i+k]) (use -1 beyond the end), assign new ranks (equal pairs share a rank), double k, and stop when all ranks are different.
editorial: The prefix-doubling idea: the first 2k characters of a suffix are the first k characters of the suffix itself followed by the first k characters of the suffix that starts k positions later. If we know the rank of every suffix by its first k characters, then the pair (rank[i], rank[i+k]) is a sorting key for its first 2k characters. Equal pairs get equal new ranks.

Each round is one sort, O(n log n), and after at most ceil(log2 n) rounds all ranks are different, so the total is O(n log2 n) (O(n log n) with radix sort). Rounds can stop early as soon as every rank is unique, which happens after one round on random text but needs all log n rounds on text like "aaaa".
